findings.who: A filer, or the spouse on a joint return, is a new resident or newly work-authorized immigrant who has applied for an SSN, not an ITIN, and has no number yet. The SSN will be issued before the due date of the 2025 return, including an extension to October 15, 2026.
findings.why_no: The helper asks whether each person has an SSN or ITIN, or has applied for an ITIN. A pending SSN application is not in that list, so the person truthfully answers no. The present-tense 'have' also ignores the IRS test, which is whether the number is issued by the due date including extensions.
findings.irs_text: i8863 p. 3, Student qualifications: "5. Filers and students must have been issued a TIN by the due date of their 2025 return (including extensions)."
findings.fix: Ask: 'Do you (and your spouse, if filing jointly) have an SSN or ITIN, or will one be issued by the due date of your return, including extensions? Count a pending SSN application or a pending ITIN application (Form W-7).' Alternatively, ask again at filing time, when the number has been issued.

findings.who: A filer or spouse holds an SSN card marked 'Not valid for employment' or 'Valid for work only with DHS authorization'. This is common for some visa holders and for people who got an SSN only for benefits.
findings.why_no: The text right above the cited sentence on i1040gi p. 17 says a 'valid SSN... must be valid for employment.' A filer who reads the gate in that context may decide that their restricted SSN does not count and answer no.
findings.irs_text: i8863 p. 3: "5. Filers and students must have been issued a TIN by the due date of their 2025 return (including extensions)." Any SSN is a TIN; the employment-validity rule applies only to the CTC.
findings.fix: Add help text: 'Any SSN counts here, including one marked not valid for employment or valid only with DHS authorization. Do not use the child tax credit test.' Cite i8863 rather than the CTC/ODC tip.

findings.who: A filer or spouse has an ITIN that expired, for example from non-use in three consecutive years, and has not yet filed a renewal Form W-7.
findings.why_no: The filer reads 'have an ITIN' as having a currently valid one and answers no. They also do not treat a renewal as 'applied for an ITIN', so they never file the renewal that would keep the credit.
findings.irs_text: i8863 p. 3: "Filers and students must have been issued a TIN by the due date of their 2025 return (including extensions)."
findings.fix: Add help text: 'An expired ITIN counts if you renew it (Form W-7 renewal) with or before this return. Answer yes if you have renewed it or are renewing it.'

findings.who: Any filer who reaches the education credit section. The gate's citation and wording come from the credit for other dependents, not from the AOC rule.
findings.why_no: A filer who sees the gate framed around claiming the credit for other dependents may decide it does not apply to them, since they have no dependents, and answer no or skip it. The AOC line then becomes false.
findings.irs_text: i8863 p. 3: "5. Filers and students must have been issued a TIN by the due date of their 2025 return (including extensions)."
findings.fix: Cite i8863 p. 3 requirement 5 for this gate, and word it with no reference to dependents or the CTC/ODC.

locators: p. 17, Before you begin, "If you want to claim the credit for other dependents, you, and your spouse if filing jointly, must have either an SSN or ITIN"
p. 3, Student qualifications, "5. Filers and students must have been issued a TIN by the due date of their 2025 return (including extensions)."
p. 4, Student qualifications, "7. You must provide the educational institution’s employer identification number (EIN) on your Form 8863."

findings.who: A registered domestic partner in California, Nevada, or Washington who files single or head of household and has never been married.
findings.why_no: The gate requires a possible marriage; an RDP is not married for federal tax purposes, and the gated question asks only about a husband or wife, so the truthful answer is no or no spouse.
findings.irs_text: p555 p. 2: 'RDPs in Nevada, Washington, or California must generally follow state community property laws and report half the combined community income of the individual and his or her RDP.'
findings.fix: Treat an RDP in a community property state as within the gate and ask about the RDP's domicile, not only a husband or wife.

findings.who: A married filer whose spouse or RDP is domiciled in a foreign country with community property law, or a filer and spouse with different domiciles one of which is such a foreign country.
findings.why_no: The question lists only nine U.S. states; the spouse did not live in or have a permanent home in any listed state, so the filer answers no.
findings.irs_text: p555 p. 2: 'The law of the state, or the law of the foreign country, where you are domiciled will determine if you have community property, community income, or both.'
findings.fix: Ask whether either spouse or RDP was domiciled in any community property jurisdiction, including a foreign country, or add an 'other foreign community property country' branch.

findings.who: A married filer who is domiciled in a community property state but whose spouse or RDP is domiciled in a non-community-property state.
findings.why_no: The question asks only whether the husband or wife lived in or had a permanent home in a listed state; the spouse did not, so the filer answers no even though the filer's own domicile is in a community property state.
findings.irs_text: p555 p. 2: 'If you and your spouse (or your RDP) have different domiciles, check the laws of each to see if you have community property, community income, or both.'
findings.fix: Ask about either spouse's or RDP's domicile, including the filer's own, not just the husband's or wife's.

findings.who: A married filer who now lives in a non-community-property state and receives a civil service annuity or military retirement pay based on service performed while married and domiciled in a community property state in an earlier year.
findings.why_no: The question asks only about 2025 while married; the spouse did not live in or have a permanent home in a listed state in 2025, so the filer answers no.
findings.irs_text: p555 p. 6: 'Even if you now live in a noncommunity property state and you receive a civil service annuity, it may be community income if it is based on services you performed while married ... and domiciled in a community property state.' Also p555 p. 6: military retirement pay is community income when based on services performed during marriage and domicile in a community property state.
findings.fix: Ask about domicile during prior years of marriage or service, especially when retirement pay is received, or separately ask whether any retirement pay is based on service in a community property state.

findings.who: A filer, including a qualifying surviving spouse, who in 2025 sells property inherited from a spouse or RDP who had lived in a community property state and whose domicile affects the inherited basis.
findings.why_no: The gate excludes qualifying surviving spouse, and the question asks only whether the husband or wife lived in or had a permanent home in a listed state in 2025 while married; a deceased spouse or an earlier-year domicile makes the truthful answer no.
findings.irs_text: p555 p. 2: 'Community property laws also affect your basis in property you inherit from a married person who lived in a community property state.'
findings.fix: Do not exclude qualifying surviving spouse from the community-property or basis question; ask separately whether the filer inherited property from a spouse or RDP who was domiciled in a community property state, regardless of the year.

findings.who: A filer who was married earlier in 2025 but divorced or widowed by year-end and now files as single or head of household, or as married filing jointly for the year of death.
findings.why_no: They read 'husband or wife' as the current spouse and answer no because they have no current husband or wife, although the question says 'while you were married' and the former or deceased spouse lived in a listed state during the marriage.
findings.irs_text: p555 p. 2: 'If you and your spouse (or your RDP) have different domiciles, check the laws of each to see if you have community property, community income, or both.'
findings.fix: Say 'your spouse or former spouse, including a deceased spouse, at any time during 2025 while you were married' and add a help example for divorce or death during the year.

findings.who: A filer whose spouse or RDP did live in or have a permanent home in a listed community property state in 2025 while married, but who wants to finish the electronic interview.
findings.why_no: The help says 'A Yes ends the interview here'; the filer reads a yes as aborting or refusing the return, so they answer no to keep going.
findings.irs_text: p555 p. 2: 'If you and your spouse (or your RDP) have different domiciles, check the laws of each to see if you have community property, community income, or both.'
findings.fix: Remove the warning that a yes ends the interview or explain that a yes opens the required community-property questions; do not make the truthful answer appear to terminate the return.

findings.who: A single or joint filer who claims only the credit for other dependents (for example, for a dependent parent or a 17-year-old child) and has enough tax liability to use the full ODC, and whose own or spouse's ODC/CTC was denied or reduced after 2015.
findings.why_no: The gate computes only 'Schedule 8812 line 8 > line 11'; on an ODC-only return line 8 is not greater than line 11 because line 11 carries the ODC amount, so the tool treats the gate as false and never asks about the earlier disallowance.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 39: 'You must file Form 8862 to claim ... credit for other dependents if your ... credit for other dependents for a year after 2015 was denied or reduced ...'; i1040s8812 p. 2: 'If your CTC, ACTC, or ODC for a year after 2015 was denied or reduced ... you must attach Form 8862 ...'
findings.fix: Gate on any positive CTC, ODC, ACTC, or EIC claim, including ODC-only; do not use line 8 > line 11. Test the dependents' credit boxes and any positive credit amount, and ask the disallowance question whenever Form 8862 could be required.

findings.who: A filer otherwise eligible for the earned income credit who elects to have the IRS figure the EIC by entering 'EIC' on line 27a, and who had an EIC reduced or disallowed after 1996.
findings.why_no: The gate helper counts EIC as claimed only if Steps 1-5 are passed and the credit computed in Worksheet A line 6 or Worksheet B line 11 is more than zero; choosing 'Yes' in Step 6 to have the IRS figure the credit bypasses those worksheets, so the helper is false and the question is not asked.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 43: 'To have the IRS figure your EIC ... Enter “EIC” on the dotted line next to line 27a ... If your EIC for a year after 1996 was reduced or disallowed, see Form 8862, who must file'; and 'You must file Form 8862 if your EIC for a year after 1996 was reduced or disallowed ...'
findings.fix: Treat an explicit EIC claim or a line 27a 'EIC' election as claimed regardless of whether the tool computes a worksheet amount; ask the prior-disallowance question before refusing or computing the EIC.

findings.who: A never-married filer who is a registered domestic partner in California, Nevada, or Washington and files as single or head of household.
findings.why_no: The gate asks 'Have you ever been married?' and the filer truthfully answers no because a registered domestic partnership or civil union is not a marriage for federal tax; Pub. 501 says such relationships are not lawfully married.
findings.line: household.cp_married_if_ever_married (and the Form 8958/community-income inquiry it gates)
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 23: 'Nevada, Washington, and California domestic partners. A registered domestic partner in Nevada, Washington, or California must generally report half the combined community income of the individual and their domestic partner.'
findings.fix: Broaden the gate/line to cover registered domestic partners in community property states, or ask a separate community-property/RDP question regardless of marriage; do not condition Form 8958 on 'ever married' alone.

findings.who: A filer in a state-recognized common-law marriage who files as single or head of household and has no marriage license or ceremony.
findings.why_no: They read 'Have you ever been married?' as requiring a formal marriage and answer no; the rule that a recognized common-law marriage counts appears only in the gated help for household.married, which is never shown.
findings.line: household.married (and any status or HSA/refusal it gates)
findings.irs_text: p501 p. 6: 'You are living together in a common law marriage recognized in the state where you now live or in the state where the common law marriage began.'
findings.fix: Put the common-law rule in the gate/help or replace the gate with a fact question: 'Did you and a partner live together in a state-recognized common-law marriage?'

findings.who: A filer whose husband or wife died in 2025 and who did not remarry. They choose single or head of household because they have no spouse at year end.
findings.why_no: "Were you married at the end of 2025?" is literally false for them, since the spouse was dead on December 31, so they truthfully answer No. The tool then treats them as unmarried and never applies the considered-unmarried test, which would refuse single or head of household status.
findings.irs_text: p501 p. 6, Spouse died during the year: "If your spouse died during the year, you are considered married for the whole year for filing status purposes."
findings.fix: Ask "On December 31, 2025, were you married, or did your husband or wife die during 2025 (and you did not remarry)? If your spouse died in 2025, answer Yes." Alternatively, add a separate gate question "Did your husband or wife die in 2025?" that also sets married to true.

findings.who: A filer living in a common law marriage recognized where they live or where it began, with no ceremony or license. They file as head of household with a child.
findings.why_no: They do not think of themselves as "married" and may also say they have "never been married", so they answer No to both the possibility helper and the question. The tool never asks whether they are considered unmarried.
findings.irs_text: p501 p. 6, Considered married: "You are living together in a common law marriage recognized in the state where you now live or in the state where the common law marriage began."
findings.fix: Add to the question or its help: "Count a common law marriage recognized in the state where you live or where it began." Ask the possibility helper the same way.

findings.who: A filer who is separated from their spouse but has no decree of divorce or separate maintenance, only an informal or written separation agreement. They live apart and file as single or head of household.
findings.why_no: Separated people commonly describe themselves as "not married" or "separated, not married", so they answer No. The tool then skips the live-apart tests, which they may fail, for example by not keeping up the child's home for more than half the year.
findings.irs_text: p501 p. 6, Considered married: "You are married and living apart but not legally separated under a decree of divorce or separate maintenance."
findings.fix: Add help: "Answer Yes if you were separated but had no final decree of divorce or separate maintenance by December 31, 2025, even if you lived apart or have a separation agreement."

findings.who: A filer whose divorce was granted only by an interlocutory (not final) decree at the end of 2025. They consider themselves divorced.
findings.why_no: They read "married" as excluding a pending or granted-but-not-final divorce, so they answer No.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 13, Single: "But if, at the end of 2025, your divorce wasn't final (an interlocutory decree), you are considered married and can't check the box."; p501 p. 6: "You are separated under an interlocutory (not final) decree of divorce."
findings.fix: Add help: "If your divorce was not final on December 31, 2025 (an interlocutory decree), answer Yes."

findings.who: A couple who divorced in 2025 solely to file as unmarried and who remarry each other in 2026.
findings.why_no: They hold a final divorce decree at year end and truthfully answer No.
findings.irs_text: p501 p. 6, Divorce and remarriage: "you and your spouse must file as married individuals in both years."
findings.fix: Add help: "If you divorced in 2025 only to file as unmarried and remarried (or plan to remarry) the same person in 2026, answer Yes."

findings.who: A filer married abroad or under tribal law, or married in a state other than the one where they now live, who doubts that the marriage counts in the United States.
findings.why_no: They assume a foreign, tribal, or out-of-state marriage is not recognized where they live and answer No.
findings.irs_text: p501 p. 6, Definition of marriage: "recognized for federal tax purposes if the marriage is recognized by the state or territory of the United States in which the marriage is entered into, regardless of legal residence."
findings.fix: Add help: "A marriage entered into in any U.S. state, or abroad or under tribal law where at least one state would recognize it, counts wherever you now live."

findings.who: A married filer who lived apart from their spouse for the last six months of 2025 and therefore files as head of household (considered unmarried) rather than married filing separately.
findings.why_no: The gate is only Filing status married filing separately. Their filing status is HOH, so the computed gate is false and the living-with-spouse question is never shown.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 15, Married persons who live apart: "You lived apart from your spouse for the last 6 months of 2025."
findings.fix: Ask the living-with-spouse question whenever a married filer is not filing jointly and a lived-apart test can matter (HOH/considered unmarried, EIC, line 6d), not only when the status is MFS.

findings.who: A married filer on a separate return who files HOH rather than MFS (for example, considered unmarried because of a nonresident-alien spouse or because they lived apart) and claims a child who could also be the spouse's qualifying child; the spouse is the only other person who could claim the child.
findings.why_no: The gate is only MFS, so a HOH separate return never reaches the question; the tool forces the line false even though the filer is married and not filing jointly.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 17, Step 1: "If the child meets the conditions to be a qualifying child of any other person (other than your spouse if filing jointly) for 2025..."
findings.fix: Gate on any married filer who is not filing jointly (MFS, HOH, or other separate-return status), because the spouse is excluded only on a joint return.
